title: Customer Care & Respectful Communication
subtitle: Serve every customer with dignity, from the first greeting to a fair answer to a complaint and a follow-up that brings them back.
description: A practical beginner course on treating customers with respect at the counter, on the phone and in messages. You will learn respectful greetings and tone, careful listening, the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence for complaints, how to say no and handle rude customers safely, inclusive service for every customer, and simple records that show whether your care is improving.
outcomes: Greet and serve customers with respectful words, titles, tone and body language suited to a Nigerian setting
Listen actively and confirm orders accurately, in person and by phone
Handle a complaint with the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence and follow up
Say no and set limits with rude or abusive customers while staying respectful and safe
Serve older customers, people with disabilities and customers who cannot read with dignity, and protect customer information
Keep a simple care notebook, calculate promise-kept and resolution rates, and build a 90-day care habit
audience: Women who serve customers in a shop, stall, salon, kitchen, POS stand or job, and want every customer to leave feeling respected.
tools: A mobile phone (calls, WhatsApp and a notes or voice recorder app)
An exercise book and pen for your care notebook
A small card for your phrases and service standards
A friend or family member to practise conversations with

modules.title: Foundations: Moments, Words and Readiness
modules.overview: Customer care happens in small moments: the greeting, the wait, the exchange and the goodbye. This module shows you how to see those moments clearly, how to speak with respect in a Nigerian setting, and how to prepare your body, your emotions and your workspace before the first customer arrives.

lessons.title: Customer care as a chain of moments: arrive, wait, serve, leave
objectives: Explain the difference between customer service and customer care
Name the four moments every customer passes through
Score a real customer visit moment by moment
Choose one low-cost fix for your weakest moment

blocks.text: **Customer service** is the task: selling the bread, plaiting the hair, sending the money. **Customer care** is how the person is treated while the task happens. Two shops can do the same task equally well, yet a customer walks out of one feeling respected and out of the other feeling like a nuisance. This course is about that second part, which you control fully and which usually costs nothing.

blocks.name: happy-customer
blocks.alt: A smiling customer leaving a shop with a purchase
blocks.caption: A customer leaves happy when every moment of the visit, not only the sale, felt respectful.

blocks.text: A helpful way to see customer care is as a chain of moments. Service experts call these **moments of truth**, a phrase made popular by the airline manager Jan Carlzon: any short moment when a customer meets your business and forms an opinion. A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. If the hairdo is beautiful but the customer was ignored for twenty minutes on arrival, she remembers both.
The four moments

blocks.title: The four moments of a customer visit
items: Arrive and greet
Wait
Serve and pay
Leave and after
blocks.caption: Every visit, call or chat passes through these four moments, and each one can be done well or badly.

head: Moment
What the customer notices
Good practice
Common failure
rows: Am I seen? Am I welcome?
Greet within a few seconds, even if busy: 'Good morning Ma, I'll be with you shortly'
Staff keep chatting or pressing phones
How long? Have I been forgotten?
Give an honest time estimate, offer a seat, keep queue order
Serving a friend who came later
Do they understand what I want? Is the price clear?
Listen fully, confirm the order, state the price before work starts
Price changes at the end, rushed or rude tone
Was I appreciated? Can I come back?
Thank them by name, check they are satisfied, follow up if needed
No goodbye, change thrown on the counter

blocks.text: The same four moments apply on the phone and on WhatsApp. The greeting is your first reply. The wait is the time before you answer. The exchange is the order or the question. The goodbye is how you close the chat and whether you check back later.
Scoring a visit

You can turn this into a simple check. Score each moment **0** (poor), **1** (acceptable) or **2** (good). Four moments give a maximum of 8. You do not need a perfect 8 every time, but you want to know which moment is letting you down most often.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring a Saturday at a hair salon
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small salon in Enugu with one assistant. A regular customer, Ada, arrives at 10:00 for an appointment.
steps: Arrive: Ngozi is on the phone and the assistant is sweeping. Nobody greets Ada for about five minutes. Score 0.
Wait: when Ngozi notices her, she apologises and says honestly that she needs 15 more minutes to finish another client. She offers water and a seat. Score 2.

Serve and pay: Ngozi confirms the style and the price (about ₦12,000, agreed before starting). The work is good, but she and the assistant talk loudly in a language Ada does not speak for most of the session. Score 1.
Leave: Ngozi thanks Ada, but does not check whether she is happy with the edges, and Ada leaves quietly. Score 1.
Total: 0 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 out of 8. The weakest moment is the greeting.
blocks.result: Ngozi decides on one fix that costs nothing: whoever is nearest the door says 'Welcome, I'll be with you soon' the moment anyone enters, even mid-call. One rule moves her weakest moment from 0 towards 2.

blocks.title: Fix one moment at a time
blocks.text: Trying to change everything at once rarely lasts. Find your weakest moment, choose one small rule for it, and keep that rule for two weeks before moving on.
What customer care is not

items: It is not flattery or calling everyone 'my darling'. Respect is calm and sincere.
It is not saying yes to everything. You can refuse a request and still treat the person with dignity (Module 2 shows how).
It is not a cover for a weak product. Good care keeps customers while you fix problems, but it cannot replace a product that does not work.
It is not only for big companies. A roadside stall has the same four moments as a bank hall.

blocks.text: Care also includes what happens when you are not there. Is the price list visible? Is the counter clean? Can a customer find your number? These quiet details form part of the greeting before you ever speak.
Where to start if you work alone

If you run the business alone, the weakest moment is often the wait, because you cannot serve two people at once. A few habits help. Acknowledge the second customer with eye contact and a word. Tell them honestly how long you will be. If the wait will be long, offer a choice: wait, come back at a stated time, or leave their order with you and collect later. A customer who chooses to wait feels very differently from one who is simply left standing.

blocks.title: Keep it honest
blocks.text: When you score your own visits, score what actually happened, not what you meant to do. The point is to find where to improve, not to grade yourself well.

takeaways: Service is the task; care is how the person is treated during it.
Every visit passes through four moments: arrive, wait, serve and pay, leave.
Score each moment 0 to 2 to find your weakest link.
Fix one moment with one simple rule, then keep it for two weeks.

activity.title: Score three real visits
steps: Copy the four moments into your notebook as four columns.
During your next three customer visits, calls or chats, score each moment 0, 1 or 2 straight afterwards.
Add up each visit out of 8 and circle the moment with the lowest total across all three.
Write one simple rule that would improve that moment, and start using it tomorrow.
activity.evidence: A notebook page or photo showing the three scored visits and your one new rule.

lessons.title: Respectful greetings, titles and tone in a Nigerian setting
objectives: Greet customers in a way that fits age, time of day and setting
Use titles and names that customers find respectful
Rewrite curt phrases into polite, clear ones
Control your tone of voice, speed and volume

blocks.text: In most Nigerian communities, the greeting is not a small thing. Many customers judge your whole business by how you greet them, especially older customers. A warm greeting tells the customer: I see you, and you matter here. A missing greeting can feel like an insult, even when you did not mean one.

blocks.name: conversation
blocks.alt: Two people talking politely face to face
blocks.caption: Respect is built from the first words: the greeting, the title and the tone.

blocks.title: Layers of respectful communication
items: Greeting
Title and name
Polite words
Tone of voice
Body language
blocks.caption: Start from a proper greeting at the top, and support it with the right title, words, tone and body language.

blocks.text: Greetings that fit the person

items: **Time of day:** 'Good morning', 'Good afternoon', 'Good evening'. It sounds simple, but a plain 'Yes?' or 'What do you want?' starts the visit badly.

**Local languages:** if you speak the customer's language well, a greeting in it can feel warm, for example Yoruba 'E kaaro' (good morning), Hausa 'Ina kwana' (good morning) or 'Sannu' (hello), Igbo 'Ndewo' (greetings) or 'Ututu oma' (good morning). If you do not speak it well, use polite English or Pidgin instead of guessing.
**Age:** many customers expect extra respect for elders. Adding 'Ma' or 'Sir' and greeting first, before they greet you, is widely appreciated.
**Religion and custom:** some customers prefer not to shake hands with someone of the opposite sex. Let the customer offer a hand first; a smile and a nod are always safe.

blocks.text: Titles and names

Titles carry weight. 'Ma', 'Sir', 'Aunty', 'Madam', 'Alhaji', 'Alhaja', 'Chief', 'Pastor' or 'Dr' can all show respect when they fit. If a customer introduces themselves as 'Dr Okafor', use that. If you are unsure, 'Ma' or 'Sir' is safe. Once you know a regular customer's name, use it: people warm up when they are remembered. Avoid 'this woman', 'oga customer', 'baby' or 'my dear' with adults you do not know well. Some find them friendly; many find them disrespectful.
Words: from curt to respectful

head: Curt version
Respectful version
rows: We've sold out of that one, Ma. A new stock arrives on Thursday. Can I show you something similar today?
Please give me two minutes, Sir. I'm finishing with this customer.
I'm sorry, I can't reduce this one. It's already our lowest price. I can show you a smaller size.
Thank you for telling me. Let me make sure I have it right this time.
Good afternoon, who's next please? Thank you for waiting.
I'm with a customer now. Can I call you back by 3 o'clock?

blocks.text: Notice the pattern. Each respectful version keeps the same facts, but adds three things: a polite word (please, sorry, thank you), a reason or a time, and where possible an alternative. You are still saying no, or wait, but the customer keeps their dignity.
Tone of voice

Customers often remember how you sounded more than what you said. Three things shape tone: **speed** (rushing sounds like you want them gone), **volume** (shouting across a shop feels rude, even when you are just busy) and **pitch** (a flat, bored voice sounds uninterested). On the phone and in voice notes, tone is almost everything, because the customer cannot see your face. Many people find that smiling while they speak makes their voice sound warmer.

blocks.title: Worked example: rewriting five counter phrases
blocks.context: For example, Tunde runs a phone accessories stall at a busy Lagos market. A friend who shops there told him he sounds harsh, so he writes down the five phrases he uses most.
steps: He records himself on his phone for one busy hour (with his own voice only, no customer recorded) and lists the phrases he hears most: 'What do you want?', 'No change', 'It's not working, bring it back later', 'Price is price', 'Next'.

He rewrites each one using polite word + reason or time + alternative. 'No change' becomes 'Sorry Sir, I don't have change for ₦5,000 right now. Can you pay by transfer, or shall I hold the charger while you get smaller notes?'
He sticks the five new phrases on a card under his counter.
For one week he counts how many times he catches himself using an old phrase. Day 1: 9 times. Day 7: 2 times.
blocks.result: The words take practice, but by the end of the week the new phrases come naturally, and the friend notices the difference without being told.

blocks.text: Goodbyes matter as much as greetings. A simple 'Thank you, Ma. Greet the family for me' or 'Thank you, Sir, safe journey' closes the visit warmly. For a regular customer, adding something you remember, such as 'I hope the naming ceremony goes well', shows that you see her as a person and not only as money. Keep it short and sincere; customers can tell when words are only a script.

blocks.title: Match the customer's formality
blocks.text: If a customer speaks formally, stay formal. If a regular customer jokes in Pidgin, you can relax a little. Let the customer set the level, and never be less respectful than they are.

takeaways: Greet first, by time of day, with 'Ma' or 'Sir' for adults you do not know.
Use a local-language greeting only if you speak it well.
Respectful phrases add a polite word, a reason or time, and an alternative.
Speed, volume and pitch carry respect, especially on calls and voice notes.

activity.title: Your five-phrase card
steps: List the five phrases you say most often to customers.
Rewrite each one using polite word + reason or time + alternative.
Write the new phrases on a small card and keep it where you work.
For three days, tally each time you use an old phrase, and note whether the tally falls.
activity.evidence: A photo of your phrase card and your three-day tally.

lessons.title: Getting ready: body language, emotions and personal safety
objectives: Use open, respectful body language with customers
Use a short pause-and-breathe routine before difficult conversations
Separate a customer's frustration from a personal attack
Prepare your workspace so that you and your customers stay safe

blocks.text: Good customer care depends on how ready you are when the customer arrives. A tired, hungry or upset seller often snaps at the very customer she needs. A cluttered, unsafe stall puts both of you at risk. This lesson helps you check your body, your emotions and your space before you open.

blocks.name: information-desk-person-female-sign
blocks.alt: A woman at a desk raising her hand in a welcoming gesture
blocks.caption: Open, attentive body language tells a customer you are ready to help before you say a word.

blocks.text: Body language customers read

head: Area
Respectful signal
Signal to avoid
rows: Look at the customer when they speak; with elders, gentle eye contact rather than a hard stare
Looking at your phone or around the shop
Stand or sit up, turned towards the customer
Leaning back, turning away, slouching on the counter
Visible, relaxed; hand items and change over politely
Pointing a finger at the customer, throwing change down
Close enough to hear, not crowding
Chatting or scrolling while a customer waits

blocks.text: Eye contact needs some cultural care. In many Nigerian homes, a younger person shows respect to an elder by not staring directly. You do not need to stare. Look at the customer enough to show you are paying attention, then look at what you are doing for them. Handing items and money with both hands, or with the right hand, is seen as polite in many communities.
Emotional readiness

Most rudeness from sellers is not planned. It comes from tiredness, hunger, worry or a bad moment just before. Notice your own state before you serve. If you are very hungry, eat something small. If you have just had a stressful call, take ten seconds before you greet the next customer.

items: Stop. Put down what you are holding.
Breathe in slowly through your nose while you count to 4.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth while you count to 6. Repeat two or three times.
Say to yourself: 'This is about the situation, not about me.'
Greet the customer as if they are the first of the day.

blocks.text: When a customer is angry, they are usually angry at a situation: a late order, a price, a long queue, a bad day elsewhere. If you hear their anger as a personal attack, you will defend yourself and the conversation gets worse. If you hear it as information about a problem, you can help. This does not mean you must accept insults; Module 2 covers how to set limits.

Plan breaks too. If you serve customers for eight or ten hours, your patience will drop by evening. Even five minutes away from the counter, with water and something to eat, can restore it. If you work with a partner or family member, take turns. If you work alone, a sign that says 'Back in 5 minutes' with your phone number is more respectful than serving people while you are exhausted and short-tempered.
Personal safety

items: Keep a clear path to the exit and do not let a customer stand between you and it during an argument.
Keep cash out of sight, and count large amounts away from the counter.
Never argue with someone who is threatening you. Step back, call a neighbour, colleague or security, and let the item or the money go if needed. Your life is worth more.
For deliveries to new customers, go in daylight where possible, meet in a public place, and share your live location with someone you trust.
Agree a simple signal with a nearby trader or family member that means 'come now, I need help'.

blocks.title: If you feel unsafe
blocks.text: Leave the situation and get help. No sale and no complaint is worth your safety. If someone threatens or attacks you, go to a safe place and contact people you trust or the authorities.

blocks.title: Ready-to-open check
items: Ate and drank water
Phone away while serving
Price list visible
Exit path clear
Cash out of sight
Help signal agreed
blocks.caption: A one-minute check before opening protects your mood, your customers and your safety.

blocks.title: Worked example: a readiness self-audit
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells foodstuff from a shop in Port Harcourt. She often feels short-tempered by afternoon and wants to know why.
steps: She scores six questions from 1 (rarely) to 3 (always): I eat before opening (1); my phone is away when serving (2); I greet every customer first (3); I stay calm when someone complains (1); my exit and cash are safe (2); I take short breaks (2).
Her two lowest scores are eating before opening and staying calm during complaints. She suspects they are linked.
She starts bringing a small breakfast, and uses the 4-in, 6-out breathing before answering any complaint.
Two weeks later she re-scores: eating 3, calm 2, total 14 out of 18.
blocks.result: Chioma's afternoons are calmer. A simple audit showed that her temper was partly about hunger, which was easy to fix.

takeaways: Customers read your face, eyes, posture, hands and phone before your words.
Use a short breathing pause before you face a difficult customer.
Hear anger as information about a problem, not an attack on you.
Your safety comes before any sale or complaint.

activity.title: Your readiness audit
steps: Score yourself 1 to 3 on the six questions in Chioma's example.
Add your total out of 18 and circle your two lowest scores.
Choose one action for each low score and try them for one week.
Agree a help signal with someone near your workplace.
Re-score yourself after one week.
activity.evidence: Your before and after audit scores, and a note of the help signal you agreed.

quiz.q: A customer walks into a busy salon and the owner is on a call. What is the best first action?
options: Finish the call fully, then greet her
Greet her briefly straight away and say you will be with her soon
Ask the assistant to tell her to come back later
quiz.explain: The arrival moment is about being seen. A quick greeting, even mid-call, stops her feeling ignored.

quiz.q: A seller scores a visit: arrive 2, wait 0, serve 1, leave 2. What is the total and which moment should she fix first?
quiz.explain: 2 + 0 + 1 + 2 = 5 out of 8. The lowest score is the wait, so that is the weakest link.

quiz.q: Which reply is the most respectful way to say an item is sold out?
options: "We've sold out of that one, Ma. New stock comes Thursday. Can I show you something similar?"
quiz.explain: It keeps the facts but adds a polite title, a time and an alternative.

quiz.q: You want to greet a Hausa-speaking customer but you only know a few words of Hausa and are unsure of them. What should you do?
options: Greet politely in English or Pidgin instead
Ask a neighbour to greet for you
quiz.explain: A local-language greeting is warm only if you speak it well. A clear, polite greeting in a shared language is always respectful.

quiz.q: A customer starts shouting about a late order. Which thought helps you stay calm?
options: "I should shout back so they respect me."
"This is about the situation, not about me."
quiz.explain: Hearing anger as information about a problem lets you respond calmly and help, rather than defend yourself.

modules.title: Guided Practice: Listening, Complaints and Respectful Limits
modules.overview: Here you practise the three conversations that test customer care most: understanding exactly what a customer needs, turning a complaint into a fair solution with the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence, and saying no or setting limits without losing respect on either side.

lessons.title: Listening that makes customers feel heard, in person and on the phone
objectives: Name the four habits that block listening
Use open and closed questions at the right time
Paraphrase and confirm an order before acting on it
Take a phone order accurately, repeating numbers back

blocks.text: Most customer problems start with a misunderstanding: the wrong size, the wrong day, pick-up when the customer meant delivery. Careful listening prevents many complaints before they happen. It also makes customers feel respected, because being properly heard is a form of respect. **Active listening** means giving full attention, checking that you understood, and showing the customer that you did.

blocks.name: talking-on-the-phone
blocks.alt: A woman listening carefully during a phone call
blocks.caption: On the phone, the customer cannot see you nodding, so your questions and repeat-backs show that you are listening.

blocks.text: Four habits that block listening

items: **Interrupting:** jumping in before the customer finishes. You may answer the wrong question.
**Assuming:** 'I know what she wants, it's the same as last time.' Needs change.
**Rehearsing:** planning your reply instead of hearing theirs.
**Distraction:** looking at your phone, serving someone else, or chatting with a colleague while the customer speaks.

blocks.text: Questions that open and questions that close

An **open question** invites the customer to explain: 'What is the occasion?', 'How will you use it?', 'What happened?'. Use open questions at the start, to understand the need. A **closed question** has a short answer, often yes or no or a number: 'Is it for Saturday?', 'Size 40 or 41?', 'Delivery or pick-up?'. Use closed questions at the end, to pin down details. Asking only closed questions can feel like an interrogation; asking only open questions can leave details vague.
Paraphrase, then confirm

To **paraphrase** is to repeat the main point in your own words: 'So you need something light for an outdoor event, and you're worried about the heat.' The customer either says 'Yes, exactly' or corrects you. Both are good: a correction now is far cheaper than a wrong order later. Then **summarise and confirm** all the details together before you start work or take money.

blocks.title: The listening loop
items: Listen fully
Ask open questions
Paraphrase
Confirm details
blocks.caption: Go round the loop until the customer agrees that you have understood, then act.

blocks.text: Showing that you are listening

Customers cannot see inside your head, so show attention in ways they can notice. Face the customer and stop other tasks. Nod, or say small words like 'Okay', 'I see', 'Go on'. Write things down where they can see you doing it. If someone else interrupts, say 'Excuse me, I'm with this customer, I'll be with you shortly', and turn back. Each of these tells the customer that she has your full attention, which is often what an upset customer wants most.

Listen also for what is not said directly. A customer who asks 'Is this the cheapest one?' may be telling you her budget is tight. A customer who asks the same question twice may still be worried about it. Gently name it: 'It sounds like price is important today. Let me show you two options within your budget.' This is listening to the need behind the words.
Phone and voice-note listening

items: Answer with a greeting and your business name: 'Good afternoon, Mama Tolu Kitchen, how can I help?'
Keep a pen and paper or a notes app ready before you answer.
Repeat every number back: quantity, price, date, time and phone number. Say phone numbers in small groups, for example 0803 123 4567.
For voice notes, listen to the whole note before replying, and reply with a short written summary so both of you have a record.
If the line is bad, say so politely and offer to call back, rather than guessing.

blocks.title: Worked example: taking a catering order by phone
blocks.context: For example, Funmi runs a small food business in Ibadan. A customer, Mrs Adeyemi, calls to order food for a church women's meeting.
steps: Open question: 'What is the event, and how many people are you expecting?' Mrs Adeyemi explains it is a meeting of about 60 women and she wants jollof rice with chicken.
Open question: 'Is there anything the guests can't eat?' She says about 10 of the women prefer food without pepper.
Funmi paraphrases: 'So, 60 packs of jollof rice and chicken, and 10 of them without pepper.' Mrs Adeyemi corrects her: '10 of the 60, not 10 extra.' Good catch.
Closed questions: date, time, delivery or pick-up. Mrs Adeyemi says delivery to the church at 11 a.m.
Price: Funmi's current price is about ₦2,500 per pack (prices vary; this is her own price). 60 × ₦2,500 = ₦150,000. Her terms are a 50% deposit: ₦75,000 now, ₦75,000 on delivery.
She reads everything back, then sends the same summary by WhatsApp so both have it in writing.
blocks.result: Without the paraphrase, Funmi might have cooked 70 packs. The confirmation message also protects both sides if anyone forgets a detail later.

blocks.title: Write it while you hear it
blocks.text: Write the order down during the call, not afterwards. Memory changes details, especially on a busy day.

blocks.title: Silence is allowed
blocks.text: When a customer pauses, wait a moment before you speak. Many customers add the most important detail after a short pause.

takeaways: Interrupting, assuming, rehearsing and distraction all block listening.
Start with open questions, finish with closed ones.
Paraphrase, let the customer correct you, then confirm all details.
Repeat every number back and send a written summary for orders.

activity.title: One confirmed order
steps: Take your next order or detailed enquiry with a notebook open.
Ask at least two open questions before any closed ones.
Paraphrase the need out loud and note whether the customer corrected anything.
Read back all numbers and details, then send a short written summary.
activity.evidence: Your notes from the conversation and a screenshot of the summary message, with the customer's number hidden.

lessons.title: Acknowledge, understand, resolve: handling a complaint face to face
objectives: Apply the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence to a real complaint
Tell a real apology from a non-apology
Offer fair options instead of a single take-it-or-leave-it answer
Follow up to check the customer is satisfied

blocks.text: A complaint is a customer telling you something has gone wrong while there is still time to fix it. Many unhappy customers never complain; they simply stop coming. So a customer who complains is giving you a chance. Handle it well and you often keep the customer, and sometimes they become more loyal than before.

blocks.name: feedback
blocks.alt: A person giving feedback to another person
blocks.caption: A complaint is feedback you can still act on, if you respond in the right order.

blocks.title: The complaint sequence
items: Acknowledge the feeling
Understand the facts
Resolve with options
Follow up
blocks.caption: Feelings first, facts second, solution third, and a check afterwards.

blocks.text: 1. Acknowledge

Start with the person, not the facts. Thank them for telling you, show that you understand why they are upset, and apologise for their experience. 'Thank you for bringing it back, Sir. I can see this is upsetting, especially when you need it for Friday. I'm sorry.' This is **empathy**: understanding how the situation feels from their side. It is not the same as admitting every claim, and it costs nothing.
Avoid non-apologies such as 'Sorry if you feel that way' or 'Sorry, but...'. They sound like blame. A real apology names what went wrong: 'I'm sorry your shirt came back stained.'
2. Understand

Now gather the facts calmly. Look at the item. Check the receipt, ticket or chat history. Ask open questions: 'When did you notice it?', 'What would you like us to do?'. Listen fully. Do not argue or blame a staff member in front of the customer. If you need time to check, say exactly when you will come back to them.
3. Resolve

Offer fair options, ideally two, and let the customer choose. Common options are: redo the work, replace the item, a full or partial refund, or a credit for next time. Be clear about what you will do and when. Then do it. If the complaint is not valid, for example damage clearly caused after collection, explain respectfully what you can and cannot do, and still offer whatever small help you can.

Before you offer options, know your limits. Decide in advance, when you are calm, what you can afford to offer for common problems: for example, a free redo for any fault in your own work, or a refund within seven days for an unused item with its receipt. When you have decided this beforehand, you will not over-promise in the heat of the moment, and every customer gets the same fair treatment.
4. Follow up
After the fix, check back: 'Is the shirt all right now?' or a message two days later. This step turns a fixed problem into restored trust.

Say something like
Avoid
rows: Thank you for telling me. I'm sorry this happened.
That's not possible. / Who told you to...?
Can you show me? When did you notice it?
Interrupting, blaming the customer or staff
I can do A or B for you. Which do you prefer?
One option only, or vague promises
