blocks.title: Worked example: a stained agbada at a dry cleaner
blocks.context: For example, Musa runs a dry-cleaning shop in Kaduna. A customer, Mr Bello, returns angrily: his white agbada, cleaned for about ₦4,000, has a yellow stain on the sleeve, and he needs it for a wedding on Saturday.
steps: Acknowledge: 'Good afternoon, Sir. Thank you for bringing it back. I'm sorry, I can see the stain, and I know you need it for Saturday.'
Understand: Musa checks the drop-off ticket. His staff noted 'no stains' at drop-off, so the stain most likely happened in the shop. He does not argue or blame his staff in front of the customer.

Resolve: he offers two options. Option A: re-clean free of charge, ready by Thursday evening, and if the stain does not come out, a full refund of the ₦4,000. Option B: an immediate full refund of ₦4,000 if Mr Bello prefers to use another cleaner.
Mr Bello chooses option A. Musa writes the promise on a new ticket: 'Re-clean free. Ready Thursday 6 p.m. Refund ₦4,000 if stain remains.'
Follow up: on Thursday the stain is gone. Musa calls at 5 p.m. to say it is ready, and on Monday sends a message asking how the wedding went.
blocks.result: The problem cost Musa one extra cleaning, but Mr Bello leaves calm, with a written promise, and comes back the following month with three more outfits.

blocks.title: Complaints about food
blocks.text: If a customer complains that food tastes or smells off, do not argue or ask them to taste it again. Apologise, replace or refund it, and remove the rest of that batch from sale until you have checked it. Food safety comes before any argument about who is right.

takeaways: Feelings first: acknowledge and apologise for the experience.
Facts second: look, check records and ask, without blaming anyone.
Offer two fair options and let the customer choose.
Write the promise down, keep it, and follow up.

activity.title: Rewrite a defensive reply
steps: Recall a complaint you received, or one you made yourself as a customer.
Write down the reply that was actually given.
Rewrite it in four parts: acknowledge, understand (the questions you would ask), resolve (two options), follow up.
Read both versions aloud and note how each would feel to the customer.
activity.evidence: The original reply and your four-part rewrite on one page.

lessons.title: Saying no, setting limits and calming a rude customer
objectives: Say no using the no-reason-alternative pattern
Tell passive, aggressive and assertive replies apart
Use five de-escalation steps with an angry customer
Set a firm limit when a customer becomes abusive, and stay safe

blocks.text: Respectful customer care does not mean saying yes to everything. You will be asked for credit you cannot give, discounts below your cost, or favours that break your rules. You will also meet customers who shout or insult. This lesson shows how to protect your business and yourself while still treating the customer with dignity.

blocks.name: person-with-pouting-face
blocks.alt: A person with an annoyed, pouting expression
blocks.caption: An upset customer can often be calmed, and when they cannot, you can still set a respectful limit.

blocks.text: Three ways to reply

Communication experts describe three common styles. A **passive** reply gives in or avoids the issue to escape discomfort, then the seller feels used. An **aggressive** reply attacks or humiliates the customer. An **assertive** reply is honest and firm about your limit while staying polite. Assertive is the goal in customer care.

blocks.title: Passive or aggressive versus assertive
items: Passive or aggressive
Assertive
blocks.caption: Assertive replies protect both your business and the customer's dignity.

blocks.text: No, reason, alternative

A respectful no has three parts. **No:** say it clearly so there is no false hope. **Reason:** a short, honest reason, without a long defence. **Alternative:** what you can do. 'I'm sorry Ma, I can't give credit (no). I had to stop because I couldn't restock (reason). I can hold the items for you until Friday, or you can take the smaller bag today (alternative).'

blocks.title: Worked example: a credit request at a provisions shop
blocks.context: For example, Grace runs a provisions shop in Abuja. A neighbour, Mrs Okon, selects goods worth ₦12,000 and asks to pay at the end of the month. She has ₦5,000 with her today. Grace stopped giving credit after several unpaid debts.
steps: Grace greets her warmly and listens to the request without interrupting.
No and reason: 'Aunty, I'm sorry, I can't give credit anymore. When some debts weren't paid, I couldn't restock.'
Alternative 1: buy ₦5,000 of the most urgent items today. Together they choose rice and cooking oil that add up to ₦5,000.
Alternative 2: Grace sets aside the remaining ₦7,000 of goods (₦12,000 minus ₦5,000) with Mrs Okon's name on them for three days.
Grace thanks her for understanding and writes the held items in her notebook.
blocks.result: Mrs Okon is a little disappointed but not insulted. She buys what she can afford, collects the rest three days later, and keeps shopping with Grace. Grace avoids a new debt.

blocks.text: A few more phrases that keep the door open: 'That's not something I can do, but here's what I can do.' 'I understand why you're asking. My answer has to be no, and I'm sorry.' 'Let me check with my supplier and tell you by 4 p.m.' Avoid long excuses: the longer your explanation, the more it sounds like the answer could change if the customer pushes. Say the reason once, kindly, and move to the alternative.

Your rules also need to be the same for everyone. If you refuse credit to one customer but quietly give it to a friend, people notice and feel disrespected. A short written policy helps: a small sign that says 'Sorry, no credit. We accept cash and transfer' lets the sign say no before you have to, and shows it is not personal.
Calming an angry customer

items: Lower your own voice and slow down. People tend to match the volume around them.
Let them finish. Interrupting an angry person usually adds fuel.
Use their name or title and acknowledge the feeling: 'Sir, I can hear you're very frustrated.'
Move the conversation away from the crowd if you can: 'Please, let's sit here so I can sort this out properly.'
Offer a choice, which gives back a sense of control: 'I can call the supplier now, or refund you today. Which do you prefer?'

blocks.text: When respect must go both ways

Frustration is understandable. Abuse is not acceptable. Insults, threats, racist or tribal slurs, and any sexual comments or touching cross the line. Give one calm warning: 'I want to help you, but I can't continue while you insult me. Can we speak calmly?' If the abuse continues, end the conversation: 'I'm going to stop here. You can come back when we can talk calmly.' Ask a colleague or neighbour to stand with you. On WhatsApp you can stop replying and, if needed, block and report the number.

After a difficult customer leaves, take a moment for yourself. Use the breathing pause from Module 1, drink some water, and write two lines in your notebook about what happened and what you did. This record is useful if the customer comes back or if you need to report the incident, and writing it down helps many people let the moment go instead of carrying it into the next conversation.

blocks.title: Threats and violence
blocks.text: If a customer threatens you or becomes physical, do not argue or try to win. Move away to a safe place, call for help from people nearby, and let the goods or money go. You can report serious threats to the police or local authorities afterwards.

takeaways: Respectful care includes saying no clearly.
Use no, reason, alternative.
Calm anger with a low voice, the customer's name, a quiet place and a choice.
Give one calm warning for abuse, then end the conversation and stay safe.

activity.title: Three practised no's
steps: List three requests you often have to refuse (credit, discounts, rushed jobs, after-hours calls).
Write a no-reason-alternative reply for each.
Practise saying them aloud to a friend or family member who plays the customer.
Write your one-sentence warning for abusive behaviour and keep it ready.
activity.evidence: Your three written replies and your warning sentence.

quiz.q: A customer says, "I need something for my daughter's party." Which question should come first?
options: "Tell me about the party: what will she be doing and what does she like?"
quiz.explain: Open questions come first to understand the need. Closed questions about size and payment come later.

quiz.q: Funmi takes an order for 40 packs at about ₦2,500 each with a 50% deposit. How much is the deposit?
Which is a real apology?
options: "I'm sorry your cake arrived damaged. Let's fix it."
quiz.explain: A real apology names what went wrong and moves towards a fix. The others shift or dismiss the blame.

quiz.q: In the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence, what should a seller do immediately after acknowledging the customer's feelings?
options: Gather the facts: look at the item, check records, ask questions
Explain why it was not her fault
Ask the customer to come back tomorrow
quiz.explain: Understanding the facts comes second, so that the solution offered is fair and accurate.

quiz.q: A customer insults a trader repeatedly after she has given one calm warning. What should she do next?
options: Insult him back so he stops
Keep serving him quietly to avoid trouble
End the conversation calmly, get a neighbour to stand with her, and keep herself safe
Give him a discount to calm him down
quiz.explain: After one warning, ending the conversation protects her dignity and safety. Rewarding abuse or matching it makes things worse.

modules.title: Quality and Evidence: Standards, Dignity and Simple Records
modules.overview: Good intentions fade on busy days, so this module turns customer care into things you can check. You will write service standards you can keep, learn to serve every customer with dignity (including older customers, people with disabilities and people who cannot read), protect customer information, and keep a simple notebook that shows whether your care is improving.

lessons.title: Service standards a small business can actually keep
objectives: Turn vague intentions into clear, checkable standards
Write five to seven service standards for your own business
Run a fair queue, including reasonable priority
Check your standards weekly and adjust them honestly

blocks.text: A **service standard** is a promise about how you will treat every customer, written clearly enough that you can check whether you kept it. 'We give good service' is not a standard, because nobody can check it. 'We greet every customer within 10 seconds of entering' is a standard: on any day you can see whether it happened.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a large checklist
blocks.caption: Written standards turn good intentions into a short list you can check every week.

blocks.text: From vague to checkable

head: Vague intention
Checkable standard
rows: Greet every customer within 10 seconds, with 'Ma' or 'Sir' or their name
Reply to every WhatsApp message within 1 hour during opening hours (8 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
Answer calls within 5 rings, or call back within 30 minutes
Give a time estimate for every job, and message the customer as soon as it will be late
Serve in order of arrival, except for the agreed priority rule
Write every promise (date, price, refund) on the ticket or in a WhatsApp message

blocks.text: Choose numbers you can keep on your busiest day, not your quietest. A promise of a 10-minute reply that you break every market day does more harm than an honest 1-hour promise that you always keep. Customers forgive a slower standard; they remember broken promises.

Keep the list short. Five to seven standards are enough for a small business; twenty will be forgotten by the second week. Cover the four moments from Module 1: at least one standard for greeting, one for waiting, one for the exchange, and one for what happens after. Write them in plain words that a new helper could follow on her first day without asking you what they mean.
A fair queue

Queues test respect quickly. Serving a friend, a relative or a well-dressed customer ahead of others who arrived first feels insulting to everyone watching. The basic rule is **first come, first served**. Many businesses add a reasonable priority for older customers, pregnant women and people with disabilities. If you do, apply it the same way every time and say it politely so others understand: 'Excuse me, I'll quickly attend to Mama first, she can't stand for long. Thank you for your patience.'

items: If the queue is long, walk along it and greet people so they know they have been seen.
Give honest wait times: 'About 20 minutes' is better than 'Just now' when it is not just now.
If you must leave the counter, say when you will be back.
Never let anyone jump the queue because they are louder or more important.

blocks.title: A weekly standards check
items: Greeted within 10 seconds
Replied within 1 hour
Calls answered or returned
Time estimates given
Queue order kept
Promises written down
blocks.caption: Once a week, tick each standard you kept most of the time and circle any you broke.

blocks.title: Worked example: standards for a POS agent stand
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs a POS cash-withdrawal and transfer stand in Ilorin. Customers have complained about long waits and confusion when transfers fail.
steps: Bisi lists her three most common complaints: not knowing the charge in advance, long waits when the network is slow, and not knowing what happens when a transaction fails.

She writes a standard for each. 1: 'Our charges are written on the board and I say the charge before every transaction.' 2: 'If the network is down, I tell each waiting customer within 1 minute and offer to call or message them when it is back.' 3: 'If a transaction fails but money leaves your account, I give you the transaction reference in writing and explain that the reversal is handled by the bank or provider, then I check with you the next day.'
She adds two general standards: greet every customer, and serve strictly in order of arrival, with priority for older customers and anyone with a disability.
At the end of the first week she checks her notebook: of 6 network failures, she announced 5 within a minute. She circles the one miss and writes why: she was counting cash.
blocks.result: Customers still face network problems that Bisi cannot control, but they stop being surprised by charges or left guessing about failed transfers. Complaints shift from 'She ignored me' to 'The network was bad', which is honest and fair to her.

blocks.title: Do not promise what someone else controls
blocks.text: Bank reversals, courier deliveries and supplier dates depend on others. Promise what you will do (tell, check, follow up), not what they will do. 'I'll call the courier and update you by 3 p.m.' is a promise you can keep.
Making standards visible

Write your standards somewhere your customers and your helpers can see them: a small card at the counter, your WhatsApp Business description, or a printed sheet for staff. When everyone knows the standard, a new helper can follow it without you watching, and customers can remind you kindly if you slip. Review the list every three months. Drop any standard that no longer matters and tighten any you keep easily.

takeaways: A standard is a promise you can check, not a vague hope.
Pick numbers you can keep on your busiest day.
Serve in order of arrival, with a priority rule applied the same way for everyone.
Promise what you will do, not what others control.

activity.title: Write and test your standards
steps: List your three most common complaints or problem moments.
Write one checkable standard for each, plus two general standards.
Put the list where you and any helpers can see it.
At the end of one week, tick or circle each standard and write one reason for any miss.
activity.evidence: A photo of your written standards and your end-of-week ticks.

lessons.title: Dignity for every customer: inclusion, fairness and privacy
objectives: Serve older customers and customers with disabilities respectfully
Explain terms to a customer who cannot read without causing shame
Treat customers fairly regardless of appearance, ethnicity or religion
Handle customer information in line with Nigeria's data protection law

blocks.text: Respect is tested most with customers who are easy to overlook: an older person who moves slowly, a customer who is blind or deaf, a wheelchair user, someone who cannot read, or someone who looks poor. Treating them with full dignity is right in itself, and other customers notice how you do it.

blocks.name: probing-cane
blocks.alt: A white probing cane used by people who are blind or have low vision
blocks.caption: Customers with disabilities expect the same respect and choice as everyone else, with sensible adjustments.

blocks.text: Two simple rules

**Ask before you help.** 'Would you like me to read the price list for you?' or 'Can I help you with the step?' Do not grab a person's arm or wheelchair. **Speak to the customer, not their companion.** If a deaf customer comes with a friend, or a wheelchair user comes with a family member, address the customer directly. They are the one buying.

blocks.title: Assuming versus asking
items: Assuming
Asking
blocks.caption: Asking keeps the customer in control; assuming takes it away, even when meant kindly.

head: Customer
Respectful adjustments
rows: A seat, a slower pace, clear and patient explanation, no rushing at the till
Say who you are, describe items and prices aloud, count money note by note into their hand
Face them in good light so they can see your lips, speak clearly without shouting, write or type on your phone, use simple gestures
Keep the path clear, bring items to them if the shop is narrow, sit or bend to eye level for a long conversation
Read terms and receipts aloud in private, ask them to repeat the key points, never comment on their reading

blocks.title: Worked example: a cash withdrawal for a blind customer
blocks.context: For example, Emeka, who is blind, comes to a POS stand to withdraw ₦20,000. The agent, Hauwa, has served him before.
steps: Hauwa greets him by name and says who she is: 'Good morning Mr Emeka, it's Hauwa.'
She tells him the charge before starting. Her board shows ₦200 for a ₦20,000 withdrawal (her own price; charges vary between agents).
She guides his hand to the card machine keypad only after asking, 'Shall I guide your hand to the keypad?' She turns away while he enters his PIN and never asks for it.
She pays out in ₦1,000 notes so they are all the same, counting aloud into his hand: one thousand, two thousand... up to twenty thousand, 20 notes in all.
He pays the ₦200 charge and she gives him the printed receipt and reads the amount and reference aloud.
blocks.result: Emeka leaves knowing exactly what he received and what he paid, without needing to trust blindly. Using one note type, counting aloud and never touching his PIN protects both of them.

blocks.text: Fairness for everyone

Give the same prices, patience and courtesy whatever a customer's ethnic group, religion, accent, clothing or apparent wealth. Avoid jokes about tribes or religions at your counter, even among friends, because customers overhear them. If you offer a discount, base it on a clear reason (bulk buying, a loyalty card) that applies to anyone.

Nigeria has laws in this area. The **Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018**, signed in January 2019, prohibits discrimination against persons with disabilities and set up the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities. The **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018** protects consumers, and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) receives consumer complaints. You do not need to study these laws in detail for this course, but you should know they exist and that fair, respectful treatment is expected.
Privacy: customer information is not yours to share

The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** governs how personal data is handled, and is enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission. For a small business, good practice means: collect only what you need (a name and phone number for delivery, not a customer's whole life story), keep it safe, and do not share it without permission.

items: Do not post screenshots of customer chats, receipts or addresses without hiding names and numbers, and without permission.
Do not add customers to WhatsApp groups or broadcast lists they did not agree to join.
Do not discuss one customer's purchases, debts or problems with another customer.
Never ask for a customer's PIN, password or one-time code, and look away when they enter one.
Keep your notebook and phone locked or out of reach of others.

blocks.text: If a customer does share sensitive information with you, perhaps explaining that they are buying for a sick relative or that money is tight this month, treat it as private. Do not repeat it, do not mention it next time in front of others, and do not use it to pressure a sale. Customers return to places where they feel safe being honest.

blocks.title: Gossip is a privacy breach
blocks.text: Telling a neighbour 'Mama Joy still owes me ₦8,000' may feel harmless, but it shames the customer and tells everyone that their information is not safe with you.

takeaways: Ask before helping, and speak to the customer, not the companion.
Make practical adjustments: count money aloud, write things down, read terms in private.
Same price, patience and courtesy for everyone.
Collect only the information you need, keep it safe, and never share it without permission.

activity.title: A dignity check of your business
steps: Walk through your shop or your online ordering process as if you were an older customer, a wheelchair user and someone who cannot read.
Write down one barrier you found for each.
Choose one barrier you can remove this week (a chair, a clear path, reading terms aloud) and remove it.
Check where customer numbers and details are kept and make one change to protect them.
activity.evidence: Your list of three barriers, a note or photo of the one you removed, and your privacy change.

lessons.title: Tracking your care: a simple notebook for complaints, promises and returning customers
objectives: Set up a customer care notebook with useful columns
Calculate a promise-kept rate and a same-day resolution rate
Find your most common complaint by counting categories
Turn the numbers into one specific improvement each month

blocks.text: You cannot improve what you only feel. A customer care notebook turns everyday events into simple numbers you can check each month. It does not need an app: an exercise book and a pen are enough. If you prefer, a notes app or a simple spreadsheet works too.

blocks.name: notebook
blocks.caption: An ordinary exercise book can show you, month by month, whether your customer care is really improving.

blocks.text: What to record

head: Column
What you write
Example
rows: What you promised and by when
Fill in later: did they buy again within about a month?

blocks.text: Write the entry straight after the conversation, while the details are fresh. It takes less than a minute. Use first names only, and keep the book somewhere private, because it holds customer information.

If you work with helpers, ask them to record their conversations too, or to tell you at the end of the day so you can write them in. Many problems happen when the owner is not at the counter, and a notebook that only records your own conversations will miss them. Keep the book in one agreed place so it does not get lost.

Be honest in the 'Kept?' column. It is tempting to mark a promise as kept when you delivered one day late but the customer did not complain. Mark it No. The notebook is for you, and it is only useful if it tells the truth.
Four simple numbers

items: **Promise-kept rate:** promises kept ÷ promises made × 100.
**Same-day resolution rate:** complaints resolved the same day ÷ all complaints × 100.
**Top complaint reason:** count complaints by type and see which is largest.
**Returning customers:** of the new customers in one month, how many bought again the next month.

blocks.title: The monthly care review
items: Record each day
Count at month end
Find the top problem
Fix one thing
blocks.caption: Recording only helps if you count, pick one problem and act on it, then record again.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading one month of notes
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sells made-to-order dresses in Owerri and has kept her notebook for one month.
steps: Promises: she made 40 promises and kept 34. 34 ÷ 40 = 0.85, so her promise-kept rate is 85%.
Complaints: there were 8. She resolved 6 on the same day. 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75, so her same-day resolution rate is 75%.
Complaint reasons: late delivery 4, wrong size 2, a sharp reply on WhatsApp 1, confusion about price 1. Total 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 8. Late delivery is 4 of 8, which is half of all complaints.
Looking closer, all 6 broken promises were delivery dates.
Returning customers: she served 20 new customers in the month, and 7 of them ordered again the next month. 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35, or 35%.
blocks.result: The numbers point clearly at one problem: delivery dates. Amaka decides to add two extra days to every quoted date and to message customers the moment a job is running late. Next month she will check whether late-delivery complaints fall.

blocks.title: Compare yourself with yourself
blocks.text: There is no official target for a small business. What matters is your own direction: is your promise-kept rate rising, and is your top complaint shrinking, month by month?
From numbers to one action

At the end of each month, set aside twenty minutes. Count the four numbers and write them at the top of a fresh page. Then ask three questions. What is my biggest complaint reason? What is one change that would reduce it? How will I know next month whether it worked? Choose only one action, so you can see clearly whether it made a difference. If you change five things at once, you will not know which one helped.

Common actions that come out of a review include: adding a buffer of extra days to quoted delivery dates, writing a price list so customers are not surprised, preparing a template message for late jobs, or asking a helper to take calls during the busiest hour. Each is small, specific and cheap.
Using compliments too

Record compliments as well as complaints. They show what you do well, so that you keep doing it, and they are useful evidence for your portfolio in Module 4. If a customer sends a kind message, ask whether you may keep it, and save it in a folder.

blocks.title: Numbers can mislead when they are small
blocks.text: With only a few customers, one bad day can swing a percentage a lot. If you had 3 complaints and resolved 2, that is 67%, but one more resolution would make it 100%. Look at the actual counts as well as the percentages, and compare across several months.

takeaways: A notebook with eight columns is enough to track customer care.
Promise-kept rate and same-day resolution rate are simple divisions.
Counting complaint types shows the one problem worth fixing first.
Use small numbers with care, and compare month to month.

activity.title: Start your care notebook
steps: Rule the eight columns into an exercise book or a spreadsheet.
Record every enquiry, complaint, compliment and promise for two weeks.
Calculate your promise-kept rate and same-day resolution rate.
Count your complaints by reason and write one action for the biggest one.
activity.evidence: A photo of two weeks of notebook entries (with names covered) and your calculations.

quiz.q: Which of these is a checkable service standard?
options: We reply to every WhatsApp message within 1 hour between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m.
quiz.explain: Only this one has a clear number and time window that you can check each day.

quiz.q: A wheelchair user comes into a shop with her brother. Who should the seller speak to about the purchase?
options: The customer in the wheelchair, directly
The brother, because he is standing
quiz.explain: Speak to the customer, not the companion. She is the one buying and making choices.

quiz.q: A seller made 25 promises in a month and kept 20. What is her promise-kept rate?
A POS customer's transfer fails but money has left his account. What is the best promise the agent can make?
options: "Your money will be back in one hour, I guarantee it."
"That's not my problem, go to your bank."
"Try again, it will work this time."
"Here is the transaction reference in writing. The reversal is handled by the bank, and I'll check with you tomorrow."
quiz.explain: She cannot control the bank's timing, so she promises what she can do: give the reference, explain honestly and follow up.

quiz.q: Which of these follows good privacy practice?
options: Posting a customer's chat screenshot with her number to show good reviews
Adding all customers to a promotions group without asking
Hiding names and numbers and asking permission before sharing a customer's message
Telling another customer who still owes you money
quiz.explain: Under good data protection practice, customer details are shared only with permission and with identifying details hidden.

modules.title: Portfolio and Impact: Proof, Your Story and a 90-Day Habit
modules.overview: In this final module you turn what you have practised into evidence. You will document one real customer interaction honestly, learn to tell your customer care story to an employer, client or your own customers, and build a 90-day plan for one habit that will keep your care strong long after the course ends.

lessons.title: Documenting a real customer interaction honestly
objectives: Choose a suitable real interaction for your portfolio
Write it up using a six-part case template
Show the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence clearly
Protect the customer's privacy and get permission for any evidence

blocks.text: Your portfolio is the proof that you can do what this course teaches, not just describe it. The heart of it is one real customer interaction, written up honestly. A real, imperfect case where you can show what you did and what you learned is worth far more than a perfect story that never happened.

blocks.name: portfolio
blocks.alt: A person arranging work samples in a portfolio
blocks.caption: One honest, well-documented case is the core of your customer care portfolio.

blocks.text: Choosing the interaction

items: **A complaint** you handled is ideal, because it shows the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence in action.
**A difficult enquiry**, such as a customer who could not decide or had a special need, also works well.
**A refusal** you handled respectfully (credit, discount, rush job) shows assertive care.
Choose something recent enough that you remember details, and ideally one you recorded in your care notebook.

blocks.text: If you are not yet running a business or serving customers at work, you can use an interaction from volunteering, a family business, a church or mosque event, or your cooperative. What matters is that it was real, that you were the one serving, and that you can describe what you did. A role-play can be used for practice, but say clearly in your write-up that it was a role-play.
The six-part case template

head: Part
What to write
Length
rows: Who (first name or 'a customer'), where, what they wanted
What they needed and how they felt
Your actions in order, labelled acknowledge, understand, resolve, follow up
What happened, with numbers where possible (refund, time, did they return?)
Notebook entry, message screenshot (names hidden) or written comment, with permission

blocks.title: From event to portfolio case
items: Real interaction
Notebook entry
Six-part write-up
Evidence with permission
Honest reflection
blocks.caption: Record it on the day, write it up while fresh, add evidence, then reflect.

blocks.title: Worked example: a late appointment at a braiding salon
blocks.context: For example, Halima braids hair in Kano. She documents a case from last month, when she started a customer's appointment late.
steps: Situation: a customer, Zainab, booked knotless braids for 10:00 a.m. at an agreed price of about ₦12,000. Halima's previous client overran, and Zainab's braiding started at 11:30, 90 minutes late.
Need and feeling: Zainab needed the hair done for an event that evening and was angry that nobody warned her.

What I did. Acknowledge: 'You're right, I should have told you. I'm sorry.' Understand: asked what time she had to leave (5 p.m.). Resolve: offered ₦1,500 off the price, or to rebook for the next morning with no deposit lost. Zainab chose the discount. Halima asked her assistant to help so the braids finished by 4:30 p.m.
Outcome: Zainab paid ₦12,000 minus ₦1,500 = ₦10,500, left on time and booked again three weeks later.

What I would change: by 9:30 a.m. Halima knew the earlier client would overrun. A message then, offering a later time, would have avoided the anger. She now messages any customer as soon as she expects a delay of more than 15 minutes.
Evidence: her notebook entry, and with Zainab's permission, a screenshot of Zainab's later message ('Thank you, the hair is lovely') with her number hidden.
blocks.result: The case shows the full sequence, honest numbers, a clear mistake and a specific change. That is exactly what an assessor or employer wants to see.

blocks.text: Privacy and permission

Before you use any screenshot, photo or comment from a customer, ask: 'May I use your message, with your name and number hidden, as an example of my work?' If they say no, describe the case in your own words without the screenshot. Cover or blur names, phone numbers, addresses, account numbers and faces. Use first names or 'a customer' in your write-up.

blocks.title: Do not invent or polish the facts
blocks.text: Do not change numbers, invent a happy ending, or write a compliment the customer did not give. An honest case with a mixed outcome and a clear lesson is stronger evidence than a perfect story that cannot be checked.

Write the case in plain, short sentences, in the first person: 'I greeted her', 'I checked the ticket'. Avoid general claims such as 'I always give excellent service'. Let the actions and numbers speak. When you finish, read it aloud to someone you trust and ask: 'Could you picture what happened?' If not, add the missing detail.

Pay special attention to part 5. Assessors and employers learn the most from what you would change, because it shows you can look at your own work clearly. Be specific: 'I would message earlier' is useful; 'I would do better' is not. If the outcome was poor, say so, and show what you learned from it.

blocks.title: Keep a spare case
blocks.text: Write up two cases if you can. If one turns out to lack evidence or permission, you will still have another ready for your capstone.

takeaways: Choose a real complaint, difficult enquiry or respectful refusal.
Use the six parts: situation, need, actions, outcome, change, evidence.
Label your actions with acknowledge, understand, resolve, follow up.
Ask permission and hide personal details before using any evidence.

activity.title: Write your first case
steps: Pick one real interaction from your notebook or recent memory.
Write it up using the six-part template.
Ask the customer's permission for any screenshot or comment you want to include, and hide personal details.
Read it aloud to someone you trust and add any missing detail.
activity.evidence: Your completed six-part case write-up with its evidence attached.

lessons.title: Telling your customer care story to employers, clients and customers
objectives: Structure a short story using Situation, Task, Action, Result
Back up claims with numbers from your notebook
Adapt your story for a job interview, a client and your own customers
Deliver the story in about one minute

blocks.text: Almost everyone says 'I'm good with people'. Very few can prove it. Whether you are applying for a job as a cashier, receptionist or sales attendant, pitching to a client, or simply telling your own customers why they can trust you, a short, specific story is far more convincing than a claim.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a job interview
blocks.caption: A one-minute story with real numbers shows an interviewer what you can actually do.

blocks.text: The STAR structure

Many employers ask questions like 'Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer.' A widely used way to answer is **STAR**: **Situation** (where and when), **Task** (what you had to achieve), **Action** (what you did, step by step) and **Result** (what happened, with numbers if possible). Most of the time should go on Action and Result, because that is what shows your skill.

blocks.title: The STAR story
items: Situation
Task
Action
Result
blocks.caption: Spend a short time on the set-up and most of your minute on what you did and what changed.

blocks.title: Worked example: a STAR answer for a supermarket cashier job
blocks.context: For example, Aisha worked for a year at a POS stand in Jos and is applying for a cashier role at a supermarket. The interviewer asks about a time she handled a difficult situation with customers.
steps: Situation: 'One afternoon at the POS stand where I worked, the network went down while 12 customers were waiting, and some had been there for 20 minutes.'
Task: 'I needed to keep them calm and help as many as possible without making promises I couldn't keep.'

Action: 'I told everyone straight away what had happened and that I didn't know how long it would last. I wrote down the order of the queue so nobody would lose their place. I offered customers who only needed to send money the option of paying me by transfer from their own phone, and I served the two older customers first after asking the others.'

Result: '10 of the 12 completed their transactions that afternoon. The other 2 chose to come back the next day and I served them first. No one left angry, and my manager later asked me to train a new attendant on how to handle network failures.'
Length check: spoken at a normal pace, this takes about one minute.
blocks.result: Aisha's answer is specific, includes numbers, shows respect and fairness, and does not exaggerate. It proves skills a supermarket needs: calm under pressure, honest communication and fair queuing.

blocks.text: Common mistakes in customer care stories

items: **Too much Situation:** two minutes describing the market and the weather before anything happens. Keep the set-up to one or two sentences.
**Saying 'we' throughout:** the listener wants to know what you did. Use 'I' for your own actions.
**No result:** a story that stops at 'and then I helped her' leaves the listener guessing. Say what changed.
**Blaming the customer:** describing the customer as stupid or wicked makes you sound unkind. Describe their behaviour neutrally: 'she was very upset and raised her voice'.

blocks.text: Back it up

items: **Numbers from your notebook:** 'Over three months my promise-kept rate rose from 80% to 92%.' Only use numbers you actually recorded.
**A customer's words**, used with permission: a short written comment or message, names hidden.
**A referee:** a former employer, supervisor or long-standing customer who agrees to confirm your story if contacted.
**What you learned:** one honest sentence about a mistake you corrected shows maturity and makes your story believable.

blocks.text: Adapting the story

head: Audience
What they care about
How to adapt
rows: Will she handle customers well without supervision?
STAR story, calm tone, mention following rules and fairness
Client hiring you for a service
Will she treat my customers or family well?
Short story plus your service standards and a referee
Your standards on your WhatsApp profile or a counter card, plus permitted customer comments

blocks.text: For your own customers, you rarely tell a full STAR story. Instead, let your standards and your record speak. A line in your WhatsApp Business description such as 'We reply within 1 hour, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., and we fix any fault in our work free of charge' tells customers what to expect. Then keep the promise every time.

Prepare a second, shorter story too, about a time you went beyond what was expected, such as remembering a regular customer's preference or helping an older customer home with heavy shopping. Interviewers often ask for both a difficult situation and a positive one, and having two real stories ready helps you stay calm.

blocks.title: Practise out loud
blocks.text: Say your story aloud three times, timing yourself on your phone. Aim for about one minute. Cut background details first; never cut the result.

blocks.title: Honesty protects you
blocks.text: Never claim a result you did not achieve or a job title you did not hold. Employers often call referees, and a story that does not match what they hear can cost you the job.

takeaways: Specific stories beat general claims.
Use STAR, spending most time on Action and Result.
Back stories with real notebook numbers, permitted comments and a referee.
Adapt the story for employers, clients and your own customers.

activity.title: Your one-minute story
steps: Choose the interaction from your portfolio case or another real one.
Write it in four short STAR paragraphs.
Add one number from your notebook and one sentence about what you learned.
Record yourself telling it, check the time is about one minute, and adjust.
activity.evidence: Your written STAR story and a note of your recorded time.

lessons.title: Certification check and your 90-day customer care habit plan
objectives: Check that your capstone evidence is complete
Choose one customer care habit with a clear trigger and action
Track the habit and calculate how often you did it
Set check-points at 30, 60 and 90 days

blocks.text: Finishing a course is easy to celebrate and easy to forget. What changes your business is what you still do in three months. This lesson helps you check your evidence for certification and build one customer care habit that lasts.

blocks.name: certification
blocks.alt: A person holding up a certificate
blocks.caption: Your certificate should reflect real evidence and a habit you will keep.

blocks.text: Certification evidence check

items: One documented real customer interaction using the six-part template, with honest reflection on the outcome.
A clear example of the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence (it can be the same case).
Your written service standards and at least two weeks of notebook records.
Your one-minute STAR story.
A 90-day plan naming one specific customer care habit, as described below.

blocks.text: If any item feels thin, strengthen it with real detail before you take the final quiz. A certificate backed by real evidence is something you can explain with confidence to an employer or a client.

Before you submit, check each item against three questions. Is it real, from my own work? Is it specific, with names hidden but actions and numbers clear? Is it honest, including what did not go well? If you can answer yes to all three for every item, your evidence is ready.
How habits form

A habit is easier to build when it is attached to something that already happens. Use a simple formula: **When [trigger], I will [action].** For example: 'When a customer collects an order, I will ask, "Is everything as you wanted?"' or 'When I finish a delivery, I will send a thank-you message within two hours.' The trigger reminds you; the action is small enough to do every time.

items: Choose **one** habit only. Adding more before the first is steady usually means none sticks.
Make it small and specific. 'Be nicer' is not a habit; 'greet every customer with Ma or Sir within 10 seconds' is.
Pick a habit linked to your notebook's biggest problem, so it fixes something real.
Track it with a tick each time you do it, and a mark each time you miss.

blocks.title: Your 90 days
items: Day 1: start and track
Day 30: first review
Day 60: adjust or add
Day 90: final review
blocks.caption: Three check-points turn a good intention into a habit you can prove.

blocks.title: Worked example: a follow-up habit for a small bakery
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma bakes cakes to order in Asaba. Her notebook shows few repeat orders, so she chooses a follow-up habit.
steps: Habit: 'When I deliver a cake, I will send a follow-up message within two days: "Thank you for your order. How was the cake?"'
Week 1: she delivers 14 cakes and sends 11 follow-ups. 11 ÷ 14 = 0.786, so about 79%.
Target for day 30: 90% or more. She sets a phone reminder for 7 p.m. each day to check deliveries from the day before.
Day 30 review: 52 deliveries, 48 follow-ups. 48 ÷ 52 = 0.923, about 92%. Target met.
Day 60: she keeps the habit and adds a note in each customer's contact (with permission) of the occasion date, to send a greeting next year.
Day 90: she counts repeat orders. In the first month of the plan, 4 customers reordered; in the third month, 9 did.
blocks.result: The habit is now automatic, and the increase from 4 to 9 repeat orders gives Ifeoma clear evidence that it is worth keeping. She cannot prove the habit was the only cause, but it is a sensible sign.

blocks.text: Ideas for your habit

head: If your biggest problem is...
A habit to try
rows: When anyone enters, I will greet them within 10 seconds, even if I am busy
When I quote a date, I will add two days and write it on the ticket
When I deliver, I will send a follow-up message within two days
When a complaint starts, I will breathe in for 4 and out for 6 before I speak
When a customer asks about a product, I will say the full price before we go further

blocks.title: Be honest about cause
blocks.text: When a number improves, other things may also have changed (a festive season, a new product). Say 'repeat orders rose while I used this habit' rather than claiming the habit alone caused it.
Keeping going

After 90 days, review your whole care notebook again, choose the next weakest moment, and start a new habit. Share what you learned with a friend, a helper or your cooperative group: teaching someone else is one of the best ways to keep a skill. Respect for people was always yours; these habits make sure every customer feels it.

blocks.title: Missed a day?
blocks.text: Missing once does not break a habit. Missing twice in a row starts a new pattern. If you miss, simply make sure you do it the next time the trigger happens.

takeaways: Check that every capstone item is real and complete before the final quiz.
Use 'When [trigger], I will [action]' for one small, specific habit.
Track it and calculate how often you did it.
Review at 30, 60 and 90 days, and be honest about cause and effect.

activity.title: Write your 90-day habit plan
steps: Look at your notebook and pick the problem you most want to reduce.
Write one habit using 'When [trigger], I will [action]'.
Draw a simple tracking table for the first 30 days.
Write your day 30, 60 and 90 review dates in your calendar or phone.
activity.evidence: Your written habit plan, tracking table and the three review dates.

quiz.q: Which part of the six-part case template should explain what you would do differently?
quiz.explain: Part 5, 'What I would change', holds your honest reflection and specific improvements.

quiz.q: Halima gives ₦2,000 off an ₦15,000 braiding job. What does the customer pay?
In a STAR answer, where should most of the time go?
options: Explaining why the problem was not your fault
quiz.explain: Action and Result show your skill and its effect, which is what the listener wants to hear.

quiz.q: Which is a well-formed habit for a 90-day plan?
options: "When a customer collects an order, I will ask whether everything is as they wanted."
quiz.explain: It has a clear trigger and a small, specific action that can be tracked.

quiz.q: A seller did her follow-up habit 27 times out of 30 deliveries. What is her rate?

finalQuiz.q: Which best describes the difference between customer service and customer care?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Service is the task; care is how the person is treated during it
Care is only for big companies
Service is polite; care is fast
finalQuiz.explain: Service is what you do (the sale, the hairdo); care is how the customer is treated at every moment of it.

finalQuiz.q: A customer visit scores: arrive 1, wait 1, serve 2, leave 0. Which moment should the owner fix first?
finalQuiz.explain: The goodbye scored 0, the weakest link in the chain.

finalQuiz.q: An older customer enters while you are busy. Which greeting is most respectful?
options: "Good morning Ma, please sit, I'll be with you in two minutes."
Saying nothing until you are free
finalQuiz.explain: It greets by time of day, uses a respectful title, offers a seat and gives an honest time.

finalQuiz.q: During a phone order, the customer says "Ten without pepper." What should you do before cooking?
options: Assume it means ten extra packs
Ignore it, most people like pepper
Paraphrase and confirm: "So 10 of the total packs without pepper?"
Ask them to send a voice note instead
finalQuiz.explain: Paraphrasing lets the customer correct a misunderstanding before it becomes a wrong order.

finalQuiz.q: In the complaint sequence, what comes first?
options: Acknowledging the customer's feeling and apologising for the experience
finalQuiz.explain: Feelings first: acknowledge, then understand the facts, then resolve and follow up.

finalQuiz.q: A dry cleaner charged ₦4,000 and offers a free re-clean or, if the stain remains, a full refund. If the re-clean fails, how much should the customer receive back?
finalQuiz.explain: The written promise was a full refund of the ₦4,000 charge if the stain remained.

finalQuiz.q: A customer wants ₦9,000 of goods on credit but has ₦4,000. You do not give credit. Which reply follows no-reason-alternative?
options: "Okay, take it, pay when you can."
"I'm sorry, I can't give credit, I couldn't restock when debts weren't paid. You can take ₦4,000 of the most urgent items today and I'll hold the other ₦5,000 for you."
finalQuiz.explain: It says no clearly, gives a short honest reason and offers two alternatives. ₦9,000 minus ₦4,000 leaves ₦5,000 to hold.

finalQuiz.q: A customer keeps shouting insults after your one calm warning. What next?
options: End the conversation calmly, get someone to stand with you, and keep yourself safe
finalQuiz.explain: After one warning, ending the conversation protects your dignity and safety.

options: "We answer calls within 5 rings or call back within 30 minutes."
finalQuiz.explain: It contains clear numbers, so you can check each day whether it was kept.

finalQuiz.q: A blind customer withdraws ₦10,000. Which practice is best?
options: Ask for his PIN to save time
Give the money to his companion
Pay in one note type and count aloud into his hand, never asking for his PIN
finalQuiz.explain: One note type and counting aloud lets him know exactly what he received; the PIN is always his alone.

finalQuiz.q: A seller had 10 complaints in a month and resolved 7 the same day. What is her same-day resolution rate?
Which is the best 90-day customer care habit?
options: "When I quote a delivery date, I will add two days and write it on the ticket."
finalQuiz.explain: It has a clear trigger and a specific action that can be tracked and reviewed.

capstone.title: Customer Care Interaction Portfolio
capstone.brief: A short portfolio proving that you can care for customers respectfully: one real customer interaction written up honestly with the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence, your service standards with notebook records, a one-minute STAR story, and a 90-day plan for one specific customer care habit.
steps: Write your five to seven service standards and keep a care notebook for at least two weeks.
Choose one real complaint or difficult enquiry and write it up using the six-part case template, labelling acknowledge, understand, resolve and follow up.
Add evidence with the customer's permission (screenshot with names and numbers hidden, or a written comment), or describe it in your own words if permission is refused.
Calculate your promise-kept rate and same-day resolution rate, and name your top complaint reason.
Write and time your one-minute STAR story.
Write your 90-day habit plan with a 'When [trigger], I will [action]' habit, a tracking table and review dates at days 30, 60 and 90.
evidence: Six-part case write-up of a real interaction, with honest reflection on the outcome
A clearly labelled example of the acknowledge-understand-resolve sequence
Written service standards and at least two weeks of notebook records (names covered)
Promise-kept rate, same-day resolution rate and top complaint reason, with workings
90-day habit plan with trigger, action, tracking table and review dates
